blocks.title: Home bias: Canadian evidence and the right amount of Canada / Deemed disposition at death and the spousal rollover / Talking about death and incapacity: estate conversations that do not feel morbid
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Evidence arsenal, lesson 8: Home bias: Canadian evidence and the right amount of Canada.

Canadian investors hold roughly sixty percent of their equity portfolios in Canadian stocks, according to Vanguard Canada research from 2023. Canada is about three percent of global stock market capitalization. That gap, sixty percent held against three percent available, is home bias, and it is one of the most documented behavioral patterns in finance going back to the French and Poterba studies of the 1990s.

Here is the mechanical problem. The S&P TSX Composite is roughly thirty percent financials and fifteen percent energy. Combined, that is close to half the index in two sectors. The S&P 500 by comparison is about thirty percent technology alone, with financials and energy each under ten percent. So a Canadian-heavy portfolio is not just a geography bet, it is a concentrated sector bet dressed up as a geography bet. Over the ten years ending 2023, the S&P 500 returned about twelve percent annualized in Canadian dollar terms, the TSX about eight percent. Currency did some of that work, but sector composition did more, because global tech carried the decade.

The mistake people make is defending home bias with "I understand these companies" or "the dividends are better." Understanding is not the same as diversification, and TSX dividend yields averaging three percent do not offset a forty-year drag from being underweight the sectors that actually compounded. The evidence does not say zero Canada. It says the sixty percent figure is not a plan, it is a habit, usually built from employer stock, familiarity, and avoiding currency conversion friction.

What this technique reveals: concentration risk hiding inside a home country allocation. What it cannot tell you: the right number for any one household, because that depends on CPP and OAS income already being Canadian-dollar and Canadian-economy exposed, which argues for less home bias, not more, once you count total balance sheet exposure, not just the equity sleeve.

In Thomson ONE, pull the sector weight breakdown for the TSX Composite against the MSCI World index, side by side, and look at the concentration numbers yourself before you argue this with anyone.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 30: Deemed disposition at death and the spousal rollover.

When someone dies in Canada, the Income Tax Act treats them as if they sold everything they own, the moment before death, at fair market value. That's called deemed disposition. It applies to non-registered investments, real estate other than the principal residence, shares in the private corporation, cottage property, everything except what passes to a spouse or common-law partner, or into a qualifying spousal trust. If it passes to the spouse, the deemed disposition happens at the deceased's adjusted cost base instead of fair market value, so no gain is triggered. That's the spousal rollover, under section 70(6) of the Act. Tax doesn't disappear, it defers until the surviving spouse sells or dies.

Here's a worked example. Dr. Patel owns a non-registered investment account, adjusted cost base 200,000 dollars, fair market value 650,000 dollars on the day he dies, in 2026. Unrealized gain is 450,000 dollars. With no spousal rollover, 50 percent of that gain, 225,000 dollars, gets added to his final return as taxable income, taxed at his marginal rate, which at that income level in Manitoba is around 50 percent combined federal and provincial. That's roughly 112,000 dollars of tax on his terminal return, due on the estate.

If instead the account rolls to his wife, Manitoba allows that transfer at the 200,000 dollar cost base. No gain is realized now. She inherits his cost base and the tax bill moves down the road to her eventual sale or death.

The one mistake people make: assuming the rollover is automatic and unconditional for any asset left to a spouse. It only applies if the property actually vests indefeasibly in the spouse, or in a spousal trust meeting strict conditions, within 36 months of death. A poorly drafted will, a discretionary trust that gives the spouse less than full entitlement, or assets left partly to kids, can disqualify the rollover on that portion.

Communication, lesson 30: Talking about death and incapacity: estate conversations that do not feel morbid.

Susan Bradley, who built the field of financial transitions planning, noticed something in her clients at Sudden Money Institute. The ones who had already talked through death and incapacity before a crisis hit recovered their footing in weeks. The ones who hadn't took years. The difference wasn't the money. It was whether the conversation had already happened.

Here's the mistake almost every advisor makes: they frame the conversation as being about death. It isn't. It's about control. The moment you say "let's talk about what happens if you die," the client's brain flags danger and shuts half the room down. Reframe it as "let's talk about who makes decisions if you can't," and the same content lands as competence, not doom.

Worked example. A client, 68, has a $2.1 million portfolio and a healthcare proxy he signed in 2009, seventeen years ago, naming a brother who died in 2019. You don't say "your estate plan has a problem." You say, "If you were in a hospital bed next Tuesday, who picks up the phone and tells the doctor what you'd want?" He stops. He doesn't have an answer. That silence is the work. You're not discussing mortality tables, you're surfacing a gap he can fix in one phone call to his attorney. Now the conversation has a next action instead of a feeling.

The mistake to avoid: leading with statistics. Advisors love to open with "70% of Americans don't have an updated will" (a figure Caring.com has reported in various years, including 2024). Stats make the client feel like a category, not a person, and they shut down faster than if you'd said nothing. Lead with the decision, not the data.

Communication: Pick one current client. Write the single sentence you'd use to open this topic with them, framed around control and decisions, not death. Read it aloud once before your next meeting.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Gildan Plunges, Musk Loses Billions, BCE Spends Big
blocks.script:
Gildan Activewear leads the board today. The Montreal clothing maker makes t-shirts and basics for retailers across North America. The Globe reports shares plunged twenty five percent after the company missed third quarter estimates and cut its full year revenue forecast to a range of five point four to five point five billion dollars. Higher borrowing costs and inflation hit harder than analysts expected. The tailwind is a cheap valuation after the drop. The headwind is a guidance cut investors rarely forgive quickly. An evidence based advisor tells a client this is a single stock story, not a reason to abandon a diversified equity sleeve.

Elon Musk runs Tesla and SpaceX, the electric car and rocket companies tied to his Texas business empire. He is in the news after spending nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates in this week's midterms, bets that mostly failed as Democrats took both chambers of Congress. The tailwind is his enormous personal wealth cushioning any loss. The headwind is a resurgent Democratic Congress now eyeing investigations into his companies. An advisor says political spending by a founder is noise, what matters is Tesla and SpaceX fundamentals, not who he backs.

BCE, the parent of Bell Canada, is next. The telecom giant posted third quarter results showing free cash flow falling as capital spending jumped nearly fifty percent on artificial intelligence data centres and United States fibre networks, per the Globe. Mobile subscriber growth stalled. The tailwind is a long term bet on data infrastructure demand. The headwind is a weaker dividend cushion if free cash flow keeps sliding. An advisor tells income focused clients to watch payout sustainability closely before adding to a position.

Airbnb rounds out the top names. The short term rental platform raised its revenue growth forecast, citing strong global demand and a rebound in corporate travel, the Globe reports. That stands in contrast to hotel operators and booking platforms staying cautious as higher airfares linked to the Iran war persist. The tailwind is travel demand holding up despite cost pressures. The headwind is regulatory friction in major cities limiting listings. An advisor says travel stocks are cyclical, size the position accordingly.

The Detroit Three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, get a mention through the Canadian auto sector lens. Industry experts quoted in the Globe say a Democrat controlled Congress could bring pushback against tariffs and renewed support for electric vehicle friendly policies, a potential lift for Canadian plants. The tailwind is policy relief on tariffs. The headwind is Congress gridlock delaying any real change. An advisor tells clients not to chase a sector on political hope alone.
talkingPoints: Gildan dropped twenty five percent on a guidance cut, not a broken business model.
Musk's half billion dollar political bet mostly lost, and Congress now has new power over his companies.
BCE's dividend math gets tighter as AI data centre spending eats into free cash flow.
Airbnb is still growing while hotel chains turn cautious on travel demand.
Nobody should buy automakers purely because Congress might ease tariffs.

blocks.title: Budget's Growth Incentive, RRSP Overhaul, CIRO Bars Advisor
blocks.script:
Budget 2026 landed yesterday, and the piece that actually changes your client conversations is buried in the tax measures. Ottawa's new Canada Growth Incentive lets founders, employees and outside investors shelter up to fifteen million dollars in capital gains on qualifying shares of Canadian controlled private corporations with a hundred million dollars or less in assets, held at least three years. For an incorporated business owner planning an exit, that moves after tax proceeds on a fifteen million dollar gain from about seventy one percent to ninety six percent. There's also an expanded small business rollover for reinvested proceeds, so revisit any sale timeline sitting on a client's desk this month.

On retirement, the budget proposes what's being called an RRSP for life: the account could stay open past seventy one instead of forcing a RRIF conversion, though minimum withdrawals would still start at that age. That follows CALU and the Canadian Forum for Financial Markets pushing Ottawa to raise the RRSP contribution age to seventy five. Also note the personal tax filing deadline is moving to May fifteenth. Update client calendars now, not in April.

On the regulatory side, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, CIRO, has permanently barred a British Columbia advisor who impersonated a client to mortgage that client's own home, forging transfers and loans. He's fined five hundred thousand dollars and ordered to pay over four hundred forty two thousand in disgorgement. CIRO has also scheduled a new sanctions hearing for advisor Michael Jordan MacDonnell. Useful if a client ever asks whether the regulator has teeth.

Wealthsimple launched an AI assistant called Penny that can move money, place trades and rebalance portfolios, with every transaction still needing client sign off, and the firm plans to open the tool to third party AI access by 2027. Expect independent minded clients to ask you about it.

For anyone in a life transition, a Wealth Professional report found fewer than one in three caregivers had any financial discussion or plan before the responsibility landed on them. If a client mentions an aging parent, that's your cue to start the eldercare conversation now, not during the crisis.

And on the watch list: the Bank of Canada's first rate hike in more than three years landed a week before this budget, so expect fixed income and mortgage renewal questions at your next client meeting.
talkingPoints: Fifteen million dollar capital gains exemption, three year hold, built for your owner-managed business clients.
Watch the small business rollover expansion before you lock in a sale date.
RRSP for life proposal, conversion past seventy one, but withdrawals still start then.
Tax filing deadline moving to May fifteenth, update your client calendar now.

blocks.title: Budget 2026 Lands, Debt and Trade Questions Follow
blocks.script:
Prime Minister Mark Carney tabled his second budget yesterday, and the scale is the story. The 2026 federal budget, released Thursday, says the government plans to reform the Temporary Foreign Worker Program. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne framed it around affordability and what he called economic sovereignty. On the spending side, CBC reports the budget pledges $50 billion over a decade on programs and services for Indigenous peoples in key sectors like on-reserve infrastructure, housing, education, health care, child welfare, policing and emergency management, plus more than $50 billion in bold and ambitious measures to expand Canada's electricity system. On immigration, the plan looks to maintain broad targets for permanent and temporary resident admissions while offering permanent status to up to 200,000 longtime temporary residents who have already applied, on top of the existing 380,000 annual permanent resident target.

Critics are focused on the debt side. CBC's analysis frames this as Carney betting he can borrow now and invest for growth, with risk if those bets don't pay off, leaving Canada's debt load exposed. Opposition voices argue that record spending shifts the burden onto younger Canadians who'll service the debt later, a framing you'll hear repeated in coming weeks as the fiscal tables get parsed.

Away from Ottawa, on the watch list: Elections Alberta told a legislature committee the Oct. 19 referendum cost just over $84 million to execute, with chief electoral officer Gordon McClure requesting an additional $49 million on top of the $34 million already spent from the $51-million budget for 2026-27. It's a live number for anyone watching the separatist file bleed into provincial finances.

blocks.script:
Start with the Winnipeg Jets, because what happened this week borders on disbelief. Tuesday night in Montreal, the Jets trailed the Canadiens by four goals with under three minutes left in regulation, then scored three times to force overtime and won it. The Las Vegas Raiders beat the New York Jets 38 and 33 last weekend, their second straight win, pushing them to 4 and 4 and into playoff conversation ahead of the November 10th trade deadline. ESPN's Adam Schefter reports the Raiders plan to stay buyers, not sellers, keeping Kirk Cousins and Maxx Crosby in place. They host the San Francisco 49ers Sunday.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Real estate and REITs: cap rates, FFO, and interest rate sensitivity / Trusts: testamentary, alter ego, and family trusts, and the 21 year rule / Explaining fees: the conversation most advisors avoid
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Industry structure, lesson 8: Real estate and REITs: cap rates, FFO, and interest rate sensitivity.

A real estate investment trust does not earn income the way a normal company does, and net income actively misleads you here. The reason is depreciation. Buildings get depreciated on the income statement every year, but good buildings often appreciate in real terms. So the industry built its own metric: funds from operations, FFO. Take net income, add back real estate depreciation and amortization, subtract gains on property sales. That's the cash the trust is actually generating from operating real estate.

Take a concrete case. Say a REIT reports net income of 200 million dollars, with 150 million in depreciation and amortization and a 20 million gain from selling a property. FFO equals 200 plus 150 minus 20, which is 330 million dollars. If there are 100 million shares outstanding, FFO per share is 3.30 dollars. Compare that to a reported earnings per share of maybe 2.00 dollars and you see how distorted the raw number was. In Thomson ONE, FFO and FFO per share usually sit in the REIT-specific template under the financials tab, not buried in the standard earnings line.

Now the cap rate. That's net operating income divided by property value. A cap rate of 5 percent on a building generating 10 million in net operating income implies a value of 200 million. Cap rates move inversely with long-term rates. When the 10-year Treasury yield rises, cap rates tend to follow with a lag, and implied property values fall, even if rents haven't moved yet. That's the interest rate sensitivity: REITs carry real debt, refinance on a schedule, and compete for capital against bonds yielding more.

The common mistake is using price to earnings on a REIT and concluding it looks expensive or cheap. P/E on a REIT is close to meaningless because depreciation inflates the denominator's distortion. Always reprice against FFO or price to FFO instead.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 29: Trusts: testamentary, alter ego, and family trusts, and the 21 year rule.

Every trust you set up for a client has a clock running on it, and most people never think about it until it's a problem. That clock is the 21 year rule, and it exists so people can't dodge tax forever by holding assets in a trust instead of an individual's hands.

Here's the mechanism. On every 21st anniversary of a trust's creation, the trust is deemed to have disposed of all its capital property at fair market value, and reacquired it at that same value. Any accrued gain gets taxed inside the trust, at the top marginal rate, unless the trustees distribute the assets out to beneficiaries before that date.

Three trust types you'll see constantly. A testamentary trust is created by a will, comes into existence on death, and since 2016 no longer gets graduated tax rates, except for a graduated rate estate in its first 36 months. An alter ego trust is for people 65 and older: they transfer assets in on a tax deferred rollover basis, they're the sole beneficiary while alive, and the 21 year clock starts the day it's created, not the day they die. A family trust, often used by incorporated business owners for income splitting or an estate freeze, also has the clock running from inception.

Worked example. A business owner in Winnipeg sets up a family trust in 2005 holding shares of a holding company worth 500,000 dollars at the time, now worth 3 million. The 21st anniversary lands in 2026, this year. If the trustees do nothing, the trust is deemed to sell those shares for 3 million, triggering a 2.5 million dollar capital gain taxed at the trust's top rate, roughly 50 percent in Manitoba on the taxable half. That's over 600,000 dollars in tax, inside the trust, with no beneficiary rollover available.

The one mistake: nobody diarizes the anniversary date. Trustees forget trusts aren't permanent, and a trust set up in 2005 has its deadline hit in 2026, this exact year, with no warning letter from anyone.

Communication, lesson 29: Explaining fees: the conversation most advisors avoid.

A behavioral finance researcher named Meir Statman studied why clients rate fee conversations as the moment they trust an advisor least, even when the fee is fair. His finding: it is not the number that creates suspicion, it is the framing. When advisors explain fees in isolation, as in "I charge one percent," the client's brain has nothing to compare it to except zero. Zero always wins. So the client hears a cost with no attached benefit.

Here is the fix, with real numbers. Say a client has 800,000 dollars invested, and your fee is one percent, so 8,000 dollars a year. Instead of stating that number alone, you say: "On 800,000 dollars, you're paying about 8,000 dollars this year. For that, I'm managing the allocation across fourteen holdings, rebalancing twice a year, and I ran the Monte Carlo projection last month that showed your plan holds up in 90 percent of market scenarios through 2045. If you did this yourself and got the allocation wrong by even a few percentage points over a decade, Vanguard's own research on advisor value, the Advisor's Alpha study, puts that behavioral cost at roughly 1.5 to 3 percent a year in lost returns." You're not justifying a cost. You're pricing a service against a specific alternative.

The one mistake: advisors apologize before they explain. They say "I know fees are frustrating, but..." That sentence primes the client to feel resentment before you've said a single number. Statman's research and later work by Daniel Crosby both show that the apology frame, not the fee frame, is what triggers the client to start shopping for a cheaper advisor.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pick one REIT in Thomson ONE, pull net income, depreciation, and any property sale gains from the last annual filing, and calculate FFO per share by hand. Compare it to reported EPS and note the gap.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull the trust deeds or will copies for any client files where you know a trust exists, find the settlement date, calculate the 21st anniversary, and flag any landing within the next 24 months for a planning conversation.

Communication: Write out your own fee explanation using an actual client's account size, following the exact structure above: the dollar figure, the specific service list, and one external comparison point. Say it out loud once before your next client meeting.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Earnings, Rate Hikes and a Post-Midterm World
blocks.script:
Good evening. Here's The Ten for November 5th, 2026.

The Bank of England raised interest rates today for the first time since 2023, and signalled more hikes could follow. The central bank warned inflation is likely to climb to around 5 per cent by the middle of next year, putting policymakers in the uncomfortable position of tightening even as price pressures build.

Closer to home, Canada's trade surplus widened to its highest level in more than four years in September, hitting 5.35 billion dollars. Gold and energy exports, mostly headed to the United States, did the heavy lifting.

On the political front, our Business Brief looks at how the Democratic wave in Tuesday's U.S. midterms is rippling into Canadian boardrooms, with corporate profits sitting at levels not seen since 1929, a striking backdrop for a changing Washington.

In energy, Shell has pledged more than 210 million dollars to oil exploration off the coast of Newfoundland after winning six exploration licences. The provincial regulator says it received ten successful bids in total, the largest number since 2000.

In tech, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board has put 50 million dollars into Toronto-based Beacon Software, a fast-growing AI company. It's a rare direct bet from CPPIB's growth equity arm, which has previously backed Cohere and Wealthsimple.

Earnings season rolled on. TC Energy beat profit estimates on strength in its U.S. gas pipeline business. Canadian Natural Resources topped expectations on higher oil prices and output. Nutrien, WSP Global, South Bow, MDA Space and Bombardier also reported. MDA Space posted nearly 31 million dollars in quarterly profit and raised its guidance. WSP Global's profit climbed to 333.7 million dollars on higher revenue. South Bow earned 99 million dollars, edging up from a year ago.

Bombardier raised its cash forecast and delivered 33 jets in the quarter, with revenue up 3 per cent to 2.37 billion U.S. dollars. Still, questions are mounting over how the company plans to deploy its growing cash pile.

Our commentary desk looks at what comes next after this week's midterms, dubbing it the post-Trump era, even though Trump himself still has 26 more months in office. Related commentary argues younger Canadians will ultimately foot the bill for Ottawa's spending and borrowing as the population ages.

Finally, the midterm results are raising hopes of tariff relief for Canada's aluminum sector, after 50 per cent tariffs pushed some producers to redirect shipments to Europe. Broader trade talks between Ottawa and Washington may also get new momentum.
talkingPoints: One, central banks are diverging, with the Bank of England hiking into rising inflation while other economies ease.
Two, Canada's trade numbers are being propped up by gold and energy, not broad-based strength.
Three, earnings season shows resource and infrastructure names outperforming, led by TC Energy and Canadian Natural.
Four, Bombardier's cash position is strong, but investors want clarity on capital deployment.
Five, the political shift in Washington could open a window for tariff relief on Canadian aluminum and broader trade talks.

blocks.label: Practice: Tax, Regulatory & Industry
blocks.title: PWL's New President, OAS Snags, Year-End Tax Moves
blocks.script:
Start with PWL Capital. The firm has named Ben Felix as president, while he keeps his chief investment officer title and his Rational Reminder podcast work. PWL Capital hands its chief investment officer the president title, with two leaders now splitting every decision at a firm managing more than 8 billion dollars for Canadian households. For a Winnipeg advisor, this is a signal that evidence-based, fee-only shops are formalizing succession and governance, something clients at bank wealth arms will ask you to compare against.

On OAS, Globe Advisor flags a real operational problem. Service Canada is enrolling some seniors for Old Age Security automatically at the age of 65 even though they requested a deferral, creating headaches for those who still earn income and want to maximize the pension's benefits. Advisors report Service Canada is taking up to a year or more to process their clients' deferral requests, meaning clients end up calling to reverse enrolment and figuring out what to do with payments already received. If you have clients still working past 65, check their MSCA account now, don't assume a deferral request was actioned.

Year-end tax planning for incorporated business owners. The Globe lays out mechanics worth repeating today. Buy and put assets into use before December 14, since "available for use" means a laptop still in its box at year-end won't count this year. Consider hiring family: pay a lower-income spouse or kids a reasonable salary for working in the business, the business deducts it, they pay less tax than you, and they build RRSP room and CPP eligibility. For incorporated professionals, remember the small business deduction means the tax rate on active business income averages just 10.8 per cent across Canada in 2026 and 10.6 per cent in 2027, much lower than personal tax rates anywhere in the country, so timing of bonuses versus dividends still matters, and watch for alternative minimum tax exposure before you pull the trigger.
talkingPoints: PWL Capital's Ben Felix is now president as well as CIO, a governance signal from the fee-only side.
If your client deferred OAS past 65, confirm with Service Canada directly, auto-enrolment errors are being reported.
Put new equipment into use before December 14 for it to count this tax year.
Hiring your spouse or kids in the business can shift income and build their RRSP room.
A third of Canadians couldn't cover a 2,000 dollar shock, a reminder to stress-test every plan.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Tariffs, Hangar Jobs, and Council Shake-up
blocks.script:
Premier Wab Kinew is calling on American lawmakers to drop tariffs on Canada now that Democrats have taken control of both chambers of Congress. Kinew congratulated Democrats for what he called dominating Trump in Tuesday's midterms, and his office is framing the result as an opening to push Washington on trade. For anyone with clients in export-exposed sectors, that's a storyline worth watching through the budget cycle.

Closer to home, Mayor Scott Gillingham has named his five member executive policy committee. Two rookie councillors have joined Winnipeg Mayor Scott Gillingham's inner circle, while two returning members take on new roles and finance committee chair Jeff Browaty keeps his job. That's the group setting the city's agenda, including property tax and development decisions, for the next four years.

On the jobs front, a 73,110 square foot maintenance hangar being built near Winnipeg's airport will create hundreds of jobs and the potential for more flights, according to WestJet's CEO. That's a meaningful capital investment landing right in Winnipeg's backyard.

Less positive: the Manitoba government has shut down a trucking company for a second time, the same operator tied to the deadly May crash in Brandon that prompted calls for a crackdown on companies who move jurisdictions or change names to dodge safety regulations.

Gillingham's new executive policy committee blends rookies with veterans, Browaty still chairs finance.
WestJet's new hangar near the airport means hundreds of jobs for Winnipeg.

blocks.title: Charity Rules Overhaul and Hydro's Drought Loss
blocks.script: The Canada Revenue Agency and Finance Canada have opened a consultation on overhauling the rules for registered charities. Canadian registered charities have until December 3, 2026, to weigh in on proposed changes that could reshape how charities interact with the CRA. The review touches disbursement quotas and whether the rules should be tightened where a revoked charity transfers assets to a closely related or newly established charity, thereby reducing the amount subject to the revocation tax. It also asks whether the CRA should make more information about charity audits and compliance outcomes publicly available, particularly where serious non-compliance results in a penalty, suspension or revocation. That's the biggest governance shake-up for Canadian charities in years, worth flagging to any client who sits on a board.

Watch the revocation tax changes if any client is planning a charity wind-down or merger.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: AMD's Canadian Bet, Google's AI School Backlash
blocks.script:
AMD is paying about two point nine billion US dollars for Taalas, the Toronto chip startup that builds silicon custom-wired to specific AI models. The Globe and Mail reports this ranks among the largest takeovers of a Canadian tech company ever, behind only the Ecolab purchase of CoolIT Systems in March. The Taalas team stays in Toronto, joining AMD's existing Canadian workforce. For your clients in tech or venture, this is the pattern to watch: build smart in Canada, sell to the Americans. It's good for founders and employees, less good if you want Canada to own the next Nvidia.

Google is in a public fight over AI in schools. It's letting school boards switch off its AI tools, but only if they also give up Google Search entirely. Politicians including New York's mayor and a former Federal Trade Commission chair are calling that coercive, bundling a monopoly product with AI adoption.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Menopause Costs, Dating Violence Alert, and Muscle Repair
blocks.script:
A House of Commons committee heard this week that unmanaged menopause symptoms cost Canada's economy an estimated 3.5 billion dollars a year. The Menopause Foundation and Deloitte Canada estimate about 540,000 work days are lost each year in Canada owing to managing symptoms, with women over 40 now a quarter of the labour force. For clients in that age bracket, this is a retirement planning conversation, not just a health one: reduced hours or early exits from the workforce show up directly in savings trajectories.

Separately, new pediatric guidance says a third of Canadian youth have faced dating violence, from physical and sexual abuse to online harassment. Doctors are being told to screen for it starting now.
talkingPoints: Menopause symptom costs are now a documented workforce and retirement planning issue, not just a health footnote.
One in three young Canadians report dating violence, a stat worth knowing if you have teen or young adult clients.
A new muscle repair compound showed promise in mice, early days, not a human therapy yet.

Worth flagging to clients: employer benefits plans increasingly need menopause and mental health coverage review.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Manitoba Childcare Gap, CCB Rises Slightly
blocks.script: A Winnipeg news conference this week put a number on something families already feel. The Child Care Coalition of Manitoba says the province needs 77,000 more licensed spaces to hit the national access benchmark of 59 percent coverage. Susan Prentice of the coalition says Manitoba needs to add 23,000 infant and preschool spaces and 54,000 school-age spaces to hit that target. The coalition credits the province for progress on 10 dollar a day care, new spaces, and higher wages for early childhood educators. But the gap is real, and for clients juggling parental leave timing against a return to work, waitlists are still the binding constraint, not benefit cheques. On the benefit side, the Canada Child Benefit rose two percent this past July, a smaller bump than 2025's 2.7 percent, reflecting cooling inflation.

Waitlists remain the real barrier to parents returning to work, not benefit amounts.
Canada Child Benefit rose two percent in July, smaller than last year's bump.

blocks.script:
Connor Hellebuyck, the Jets' former number one goalie now with the Devils, posted an open letter to Winnipeg fans. Per CBC Sports, he expressed gratitude to the organization, the city, and Manitoba's lakes. The Globe and Mail reports family reasons contributed to his trade request, and he acknowledges the move disappointed fans who supported him throughout his career in Winnipeg.

Bigger hockey story: Canada has barred Russia from the world juniors and other hockey events, part of a widening boycott. The Globe reports Ottawa is dismissing blowback fears, with former International Olympic Committee member Dick Pound noting the Canadian government has final say on who enters the country for the tournament in Alberta.

On football, your Raiders snapped a four-game skid, beating the Jets 38-33 in a comeback Sunday. Kirk Cousins threw three touchdown passes, and Las Vegas sits at 4-4. They travel to face the 6-1 49ers this Sunday, with the trade deadline approaching; the Athletic flags the Chiefs, Bengals, Bears and Rams as possible buyers. Monday night pits two 6-1 teams, Buffalo at Minnesota.
talkingPoints: Raiders are back to .500 heading into a tough road test at San Francisco.
